questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A small block is projected up a rough inclined plane having a slope angle θ. It is observed that the time taken by the block to slide down to its starting point is 3 times the time it takes to slide up to its highest point. Assuming the coefficients of static and kinetic friction are equal, what is the coefficient of kinetic friction μk between the block and the inclined plane?
questions.solution: Let the distance moved up the incline be s. The upward acceleration is aup = g(sinθ + μkcosθ). Thus, the time of ascent is tup = \(\frac{2s}{aup}\). When sliding down, the downward acceleration is adown = g (sinθ − μkcosθ). The time of descent is tdown = \(\frac{2s}{adown}\). Given that tdown = 3tup, squaring both sides yields aup = 9adown. Substituting the accelerations gives g (sinθ + μkcosθ) = 9g (sinθ − μkcosθ). Simplifying this equation: sinθ + μkcosθ = 9sinθ −9μkcosθ, which implies 10μkcosθ = 8sinθ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Monkey A (mass MA =10 kg ) and Monkey B (mass MB = 30 kg ) are holding onto opposite ends of a light, inextensible rope that passes over a fixed, smooth pulley. Monkey A climbs up the rope such that his upward acceleration relative to the rope is 6 \(m/s^{2}\). Simultaneously, Monkey B climbs up the rope such that his upward acceleration relative to his side of the rope is 2 \(m/s^{2}\). What is the tension in the rope? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: Let the side of the rope holding Monkey A accelerate upwards with an absolute acceleration a. The side holding Monkey B must therefore accelerate downwards with a. The absolute upward acceleration of Monkey A is aA = a + 6. The absolute upward acceleration of Monkey B is aB = −a + 2. The equation of motion for A is T − M Ag = M AaA ⇒T −100 =10(a + 6), which simplifies to T =10a +160. The equation of motion for B is T − MBg = MBaB ⇒T − 300 = 30(−a + 2), which simplifies to T = −30a + 360. Equating the expressions for tension: 10a +160 = −30a + 360 ⇒40a = 200 ⇒a = 5 \(m/s^{2}\). ⇒ T = 210 N

questions.text: A block of mass m = 2 kg is resting on a rough horizontal surface having a coefficient of static friction μs = 0.75. A pulling force F is applied to the block at an angle of 37 above the horizontal. What is the minimum value of F required to initiate the motion of the block? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) and sin37 = 3 / 5 )
questions.solution: Resolve the applied force F into horizontal and vertical components: Fx = Fcos37 = 0.8F and Fy = Fsin37 = 0.6F. The normal reaction from the surface balances vertical forces: N + Fy = mg ⇒ N = 20 − 0.6F. The maximum static friction available is fL = μsN = 0.75(20 − 0.6F ) =15 − 0.45F. To just initiate motion, the horizontal pulling Solutions force must equal the limiting static friction: Fx = fL. Equating the two yields 0.8F =15 − 0.45F ⇒ 1.25F =15. F = 12 N

questions.text: A light inextensible string passes over a smooth fixed pulley. One end of the string is attached to Block B of mass 4 kg. The other end of the string is connected to a light spring of force constant k =100 N/m, which in turn is connected to Block A of mass 2 kg hanging vertically. The system is held at rest such that the spring is extended by 10 cm. If the system is suddenly released, what are the accelerations of Block A and Block B respectively, immediately after release? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: The spring is initially extended by x = 0.1 m. The spring force is Fs = kx =100×0.1=10 N. Because the spring and the string are massless, the tension T in the string must instantly balance the spring force at their junction. Thus, T = Fs =10 Nimmediately after release. For Block A ( mA = 2 kg ), the forces are gravity ( 20 N downwards) and the spring force (10 N upwards). The net force is 20 −10 =10 N downwards. The acceleration of Block A is aA = \(\frac{10}{2}\) = 5 \(m/s^{2}\) downwards. For Block B ( mB = 4 kg ), the forces are gravity (40 N downwards) and the string tension (10 N upwards). The net force is 40 −10 = 30 N downwards. The acceleration of Block B is aB = \(\frac{30}{4}\) = 7.5 \(m/s^{2}\) downwards.

questions.text: Block A of mass 2 kg rests on Block B of mass 3 kg, which in turn rests on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between A and B is μ1 = 0.4, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between B and the floor is μ2 = 0.1. A horizontal time-varying force F = 5t (where F is in Newtons and t is in seconds) is applied to Block A. Assume static friction on the floor is matched to kinetic friction ( μs = μk = 0.1). Assuming g =10 \(m/s^{2}\), at what time t will Block A start to slip over Block B?
questions.solution: The maximum static friction between A and B is f1,max = μ1mAg = 0.4× 20 = 8 N. Kinetic friction between B and the floor is f2 = μ2 (mA + mB ) g = 0.1×50 = 5 N. The system starts moving together when F 5 N, which corresponds to t 1 s. For t 1, the common acceleration of the two blocks is a = \(\frac{F}{mA}\) \(\frac{−}{+}\) \(\frac{f2}{mB}\) = 5t\(\frac{−}{5}\) 5 = t −1. The only horizontal forward force acting on Block B is the static friction f1 exerted by Block A. The equation of motion for Block B is f1 − f2 = mBa. Substitute the known expressions: f1 − 5 = 3(t −1) ⇒ f1 = 3t − 3 + 5 ⇒ f1 = 3t + 2. Slipping between A and B begins when the required static friction f1 reaches its maximum possible value of 8 N. Therefore, 3t + 2 = 8 ⇒3t = 6 ⇒t = 2 s. and

questions.text: In the system shown, a light inextensible string is anchored to the ceiling, passes under a movable light pulley P1, then goes over a fixed light pulley P2, and is finally attached to Block A of mass 3 kg. Block B of mass 4 kg is suspended from the movable pulley P1. All segments of the string are vertical. If the system is released from rest, what is the magnitude of the downward acceleration of Block A? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: Establish the constraint. If Block B (and pulley P1 ) moves downwards by a distance y, the string segments on both sides of P1 must lengthen by y, demanding 2 y length of string. Therefore, Block A must move upwards by 2 y. Accelerations are thus aB = a (downwards) and aA = 2a (upwards). Let T be the tension in the string. The upward force on P1 (and thus on Block B) is 2T. The equation of motion for Block B is mBg − 2T = mBa ⇒40 − 2T = 4a, which simplifies to 20 − T = 2a. The equation of motion for Block A is T − mAg = mA (2a) ⇒T − 30 = 3(2a) = 6a. Substitute T = 30 + 6a into the equation for Block B: 20 − (30 + 6a) = 2a ⇒ −10 − 6a = 2a ⇒8a = −10⇒a = −1.25 \(m/s^{2}\). The negative sign means Block B accelerates upwards. Block A's upward acceleration is 2a = 2(−1.25) = −2.5 \(m/s^{2}\). Thus, Block A has a downward acceleration of 2.5 \(m/s^{2}\).

questions.text: A crate of mass 5 kg is sliding across a rough horizontal floor with a constant velocity vector \(\vec{v}\) = 4iˆ − 3 ˆj m/s. It is being simultaneously pushed by two people applying constant ° ° horizontal forces F1 and F2. The first person applies \(\vec{F}1\) =15iˆ +10 ˆj N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the floor is μk = 0.5. What is the force \(\vec{F}2\) applied by the second person? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: The crate moves with a constant velocity, which implies the net acceleration is zero and the net force is zero: \(F^{°°}1 +\) F2 + \(\vec{f}k\) = 0. ° Determine the kinetic friction vector fk. It opposes the direction of velocity. The velocity's magnitude is v = \(4^{2}\) + (\(−3)^{2}\) = 5 m/s. The unit vector for velocity is vˆ = 4 iˆ − 3 ˆj. 5 5 The magnitude of kinetic friction is fk = μkmg = 0.5×5×10 = 25 N. The kinetic friction vector is \(\vec{f}k\) = − fkvˆ = −25(\(\frac{4}{5}\) iˆ | \(\frac{3}{5}\) ˆj) = −20iˆ +15 ˆj N. Set the net force to zero: (15iˆ +10 ˆj) + \(\vec{F}2\) + (−20iˆ +15ˆj) = 0. ° Combine terms to solve for F2: (−5iˆ + 25 ˆj) + \(F^{°°}2 =\) 0⇒F2 = 5iˆ − 25 ˆj N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A small particle is constrained to move on a circular track of radius R. It starts from rest and moves with a constant tangential acceleration at. At what total angle θ (in radians) traversed by the particle will its total acceleration vector make an angle of 45with its velocity vector?
questions.solution: The particle has two components of acceleration: a constant tangential acceleration at and a varying centripetal acceleration ac. Since the particle starts from rest, its angular velocity after traversing an angle θ is given by the kinematic equation \(ω^{2}\) = 2αθ. The centripetal acceleration can be expressed as ac = \(ω^{2} R\) = (2αθ) R = 2θ(αR) = 2θat. The angle φ between the total acceleration vector and the velocity vector (which is purely tangential) is given by tanφ = ac. For φ = 45, we at must have tan45 =1, which requires ac = at.

questions.text: A car negotiates a banked circular curve of radius R = 40 m on a rough road. The road is banked at an angle θ = 45to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between the car's tires and the road surface is μs = 0.6. What is the maximum safe speed of the car to avoid skidding outwards up the incline? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: The forces acting on the car are gravity mg, normal reaction N, and static friction f pointing downwards along the incline to prevent outward skidding. Resolving forces vertically for no vertical acceleration: \(Ncos45 −^{°°}\) fsin45 = mg. At maximum safe speed, f = μsN. Thus, N \((cos45 −^{°°}\) μssin45 ) = mg. Resolving forces horizontally provides the necessary centripetal force: N\(sin45 +^{°°}\) fcos45 = \(mv^{2}\), which yields R N \((sin45 +^{°°}\) μscos45 ) = \(\frac{mv^{2}}{R}\). Dividing the horizontal equation by the vertical equation gives \(\frac{v^{2}}{Rg}\) = \(\frac{sin45 +^{°°}}{cos45 −^{°°}}\)\(\frac{μscos45}{μssin45}\) = \(\frac{1}{1}\)\(\frac{+}{−}\) \(\frac{μs}{μs}\) (since \(sin45 =^{°°}\) cos45 ). Substitute the given values ( R = 40 m, g =10 \(m/s^{2}\), μs = 0.6 ): \(\frac{v^{2}}{400}\) = \(\frac{1}{1}\)\(\frac{+}{−}\) \(\frac{0.6}{0.6}\) = \(\frac{1.6}{0.4}\) = 4.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A small ball of mass m =1.2 kg is attached to one end of a light string of length L = 0.4 m. The other end of the string is fixed to a rigid ceiling. The ball is set into uniform circular motion in a horizontal plane, forming a conical pendulum. The string will break if the tension exceeds Tmax = 48 N. What is the maximum angular velocity ω at which the ball can revolve without breaking the string? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: In a conical pendulum, the vertical component of the string's tension balances the weight of the bob: Tcosθ = mg. The horizontal component of the tension provides the centripetal force for the circular path: Tsinθ = \(mω^{2}\)R. The radius of the circular path is related to the string length by R = Lsinθ. Substituting R into the centripetal force equation gives Tsinθ = \(mω^{2}\)Lsinθ, which simplifies directly to T = \(mω^{2}\)L. To find the maximum angular velocity, we set the tension to its maximum allowed value Tmax: 48 =1.2\(×ωmax^{2}\) ×0.4.

questions.text: A uniform elastic ring of mass M = \(π^{2}\) kg and natural (unstretched) radius R0 = 3 m is placed on a smooth horizontal table. It is spun about a vertical axis passing through its center with a constant angular velocity ω = 4 rad/s. Due to the rotation, the ring expands to a new steady radius R = 4 m. Assuming the ring obeys spring law ( T = kΔL, where T is the internal tension and ΔL is the change in the ring's circumference and k is spring constant), what is the effective spring constant k of the ring?
questions.solution: The centripetal force required to keep a uniform ring of mass M in circular motion is provided by its internal tension T. The relation is T = \(\frac{M}{2π}\) \(ω^{2}\)R.. Substitute the given values into the tension formula: T = \(\frac{π^{2}}{2π}\) \((4^{2}\) )(4) = \(\frac{π}{2}\) (16)(4) = 32π N. The change in the circumference of the ring due to expansion is ΔL = 2πR − 2πR0 = 2π(4 − 3) = 2π m. According to Hooke's law, the tension is proportional to the stretch in circumference: T = kΔL. Equating the tensions gives 32π = k (2π). k = 16 N/m

questions.text: A particle of mass 1 kg moves in the x − y plane. At time t = 0, its velocity is \(\vec{v}0\) = 4iˆ + 3 ˆj m/s. \(\vec{F} =\) \(\frac{particle}{−2iˆ + ˆj}\)\(\frac{is}{N.}\) \(\frac{subjected}{At what}\) \(\frac{to a constant}{time t 0}\) \(\frac{force}{will}\)\(\frac{of}{the}\) particle's velocity vector be exactly perpendicular to its initial velocity vector?
questions.solution: The velocity of the particle at any time t under constant acceleration is given by the kinematic equation \(v^{°°°} (t)\) = v0 + at. Substituting the given vectors, we get \(\vec{v} (t)\) = (4iˆ + 3ˆj) + (−2iˆ + ˆj)t = (4 − 2t)iˆ + (3+ t) ˆj. Two vectors are perpendicular if their dot product is zero. Thus, we require \(v^{°°} (t\)) ⋅ v0 = 0. Compute the dot product: (4 − 2t)(4) + (3 + t)(3) = 0. Expand the equation: 16 − 8t + 9 + 3t = 0, which simplifies to 25 − 5t = 0.

questions.text: A car is traveling on a flat, unbanked circular track of radius R = 25 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tires and the track is μs = 0.5. At a certain instant, the driver steps on the accelerator such that the car's speed increases at a constant tangential rate of 3 \(m/s^{2}\). What is the maximum speed the car can have at this exact instant without skidding off the track? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: To prevent skidding, the total horizontal force from the road (static friction f ) must provide both the tangential acceleration ( at = 3 \(m/s^{2}\) ) and the centripetal acceleration ( ac = \(\frac{v^{2}}{R}\) ). Since these two acceleration components are perpendicular, the magnitude of the total required acceleration is a = \(at^{2}\) + \(ac^{2}\). The maximum possible total acceleration is limited by the maximum available static friction: amax = \(\frac{fmax}{m}\) = \(\frac{μsmg}{m}\) = μsg = 0.5×10 = 5 \(m/s^{2}\). Equating the required acceleration to the maximum available gives the boundary condition for skidding: \(3^{2}\) + \(ac^{2}\) = 5. Solving for the centripetal component gives 9 + \(ac^{2}\) = 25 ⇒ \(ac^{2}\) =16 ⇒ ac = 4 \(m/s^{2}\).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A small block of mass m = 2 kg is attached to one end of a light ideal super-elastic spring of natural length L0 =1 m and spring constant k =100 N/m. The other end of the spring is fixed to the center of a rough horizontal turntable. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the turntable is μs = 0.5. The turntable is rotating with a constant angular velocity ω = 5 rad/s. What is the maximum possible extension of the spring such that the block remains at rest relative to the turntable? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: Let the extension of the spring be x. The radius of the circular path is R = L0 + x =1+ x. The required centripetal force for the block is Fc = \(mω^{2} R\) = 2(25)(1+ x) = 50 + 50x N. This force must be provided by the combination of spring force and static friction acting inwards. The inward spring force is Fs = kx =100x N. The maximum available static friction is fmax = μsmg = 0.5(20) =10 N. For the maximum possible extension, the spring is pulling inwards stronger than the required centripetal force (100x 50 + 50x ). The block thus has a tendency to slide inwards. To prevent slipping, static friction must act outwards at its maximum value. The force balance equation is Fs − fmax = Fc, which translates to 100x −10 = 50 + 50x.

questions.text: A small collar of mass m = 6 kg can slide on a smooth horizontal rod. A light spring of natural length L0 = 3 m and spring constant k = 50 N/m has one end attached to a fixed point P which is at a vertical height of 4 m directly above the rod. The other end is attached to the collar. The collar is initially held at rest on the rod at a horizontal distance of 3 m from the point directly below P. If the collar is released, what is its speed when it passes through the point directly below P ?
questions.solution: Calculate the initial length of the spring. The initial horizontal distance is 3 m and vertical distance is 4 m, so the initial length is Li = \(3^{2}\) + \(4^{2}\) = 5 m. The initial extension of the spring is xi = Li − L0 = 5−3 = 2 m. The initial elastic potential energy is Ui = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(kxi^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) (50)\((2^{2}\) ) =100 J. When the collar is directly below P, the spring is vertical. Its length is Lf = 4 m. The final extension is xf = Lf − L0 = 4 − 3 =1 m. The final elastic potential energy is U f = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(kxf^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) (50)\((1^{2}\) ) = 25 J. By conservation of mechanical energy (since the rod is smooth and horizontal, gravity does no work): Ui =U f + \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(mv^{2}\). Substitute the values: 100 = 25 + \(\frac{1}{2}\) (6\()v^{2}\) ⇒75 = \(3v^{2}\) ⇒\(v^{2}\) = 25⇒ v = 5 m/s.

questions.text: A block of mass m = 5 kg is initially at rest on a rough horizontal surface with a coefficient of kinetic friction μk = 0.25. It is subjected to a horizontal driving force F ( x) that varies with its position x as shown in the given graph. The force is constant at 30 N from x = 0 to x =10 m, and then decreases linearly to 10 N at x = 20 m. What is the speed of the block when it reaches x = 20 m ? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) and assume limiting static friction is just less than 30 N )
questions.solution: Calculate the work done by the driving force F ( x), which is the area under the F − x graph from x = 0 to x = 20 m. The area consists of a rectangle from x = 0 to 10 m and a trapezoid from x =10 to 20 m. Wd = (30×10) + \(\frac{1}{2}\) (30 +10)×10 = 300 + 200 = 500 J. Calculate the constant kinetic friction force: fk = μkmg = 0.25×5×10 =12.5 N. (Since F (0) = 30 N 12.5 N, the block starts moving immediately). The work done by friction over the 20 m distance is Wf = − fk × d = −12.5× 20 = −250 J. By the work-energy theorem, the net work equals the change in kinetic energy: Wnet =Wd +Wf = 500 − 250 = 250 J. Thus, 1 \(mv^{2}\) = 250 ⇒ 2.5\(v^{2}\) = 250 2 \(v^{2}\) =100 ⇒v =10 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A vehicle of mass m =1000 kg starts from rest and is driven by an engine that delivers a constant power of P =18 kW. Assuming there are no resistive forces like friction or air drag, what is the total distance covered by the vehicle in the first 9 s of its motion?
questions.solution: The engine delivers constant power P, so the work done in time t is W = Pt. By the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy of the vehicle is equal to the work done: 1 \(mv^{2}\) = Pt. 2 Rearranging for velocity gives v(t) = \(t_{m}^{2P 1/2}\). The distance covered is the integral of velocity with respect to time: x(t) = \(|0^{t}\) \(τ_{m}^{2P 1/2} dτ\) = \(\frac{2P}{m}\) ( \(\frac{2}{3}\) \(t^{3/2}\) ). Substitute the given values ( P =18000 W and m =1000 kg ): 2P = 36000 = 36 = 6. m 1000 Calculate the distance at t = 9 s: x(9) = 6× \(\frac{2}{3}\) × \((9)^{3/2}\) = 4× 27 =108 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A block of mass m = 2.5 kg is dropped from a height H =10 m directly above an uncompressed vertical spring of spring constant k =100 N/m fixed to the ground. Assuming no air resistance and that the block attaches to the spring upon impact, what is the maximum compression of the spring? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: Let the maximum compression of the spring be x. The block falls a total vertical distance of H + x. The total loss in gravitational potential energy from the release point to the point of maximum compression is ΔUg = mg(H + x). At maximum compression, the block momentarily comes to rest, so the change in kinetic energy is zero. All lost gravitational potential energy is converted into elastic potential energy of the spring. The elastic potential energy gained by the spring is ΔUs = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(kx^{2}\). Equating the two energies: mg (H + x) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(kx^{2}\). Substitute the known values: 2.5×10×(10 + x) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) ×100× \(x^{2}\) ⇒25(10 + x) = \(50x^{2}\). Simplify to a quadratic equation: 250 + 25x = 50\(x^{2}\) ⇒ 2\(x^{2}\) − x −10 = 0. Factorize the quadratic: (2x − 5)( x + 2) = 0. Since the compression x must be positive, x = 2.5 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A particle of mass m = 4 kg moves in the x − y plane under the action of a time-varying force. The position vector of the particle as a function of time t is given by \(\vec{r} (t)\) = \((t^{3}\) − 3t)iˆ + \((2t^{2}\) − 4t) ˆj, where \(\vec{r}\) is in meters and t is in seconds. What is the total work done by the force on the particle during the time interval from t = 0 to t = 2 s ?
questions.solution: The work done by the net force is equal to the change in kinetic energy of the particle (Work- Energy Theorem): W = ΔK = \(\frac{1}{2}\) m\((v f^{2}\) − \(vi^{2}\) ). Find the velocity vector \(\vec{v}\)(t ) by differentiating the position vector \(\vec{r}\)(t ) with respect to time: \(\vec{v} (t)\) = \(\frac{\vec{dr}}{dt}\) = \((3t^{2}\) − 3)iˆ + (4t − 4) ˆj. Calculate the initial velocity vector at t = 0: \(\vec{v}\)(0) = (0 −3)iˆ + (0 − 4) ˆj = −3iˆ − 4 ˆj m/s. The square of the initial speed is \(vi^{2}\) = (\(−3)^{2}\) + (\(−4)^{2}\) = 9 +16 = 25 \((m/s)^{2}\). Calculate the final velocity vector at t = 2 s: \(\vec{v}\)(2) = (3(4) − 3)iˆ + (4(2) − 4) ˆj = 9iˆ + 4 ˆj m/s. The square of the final speed is \(vf^{2}\) = \(9^{2}\) + \(4^{2}\) = 81+16 = 97 \((m/s)^{2}\). Calculate the work done: W = \(\frac{1}{2}\) (4)(97 − 25) = 2(72) =144 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A particle moves along the x -axis under the influence of a conservative force field. Its potential energy is given by U ( x) = \(\frac{1}{4}\) \(x^{4}\) − \(2x^{2}\), where U is in Joules and x is in meters. The particle is released from rest at the position x = 4 m. What is the maximum kinetic energy (in Joules) achieved by the particle during its subsequent motion?
questions.solution: Since the particle is released from rest at x = 4 m, its total mechanical energy E is purely its initial potential energy: E =U (4) = \(\frac{1}{4}\) \((4^{4}\) ) − 2\((4^{2}\) ) = 256 − 32 = 64 − 32 = 32 J. 4 The total energy E remains constant. The kinetic energy is maximum where the potential energy is minimum, since K = E −U ( x). To find the minima of U ( x), set the derivative to zero: \(\frac{dU}{dx}\) = \(x^{3}\) − 4x = x( \(x^{2}\) − 4) = 0. The roots are x = 0 and x = ±2 m. Check the second derivative: \(\frac{d U^{2}}{dx^{2}}\) = 3\(x^{2}\) − 4. At x = 0, it is −4 (local maximum). At x = ±2, it is 3(4) − 4 = 8 0 (global minima). Calculate the minimum potential energy at x = ±2 m: Umin = \(\frac{1}{4}\) (±\(2)^{4}\) − 2(±\(2)^{2}\) = 4 − 8 = −4 J. The maximum kinetic energy is Kmax = E −Umin = 32 − (−4) = 36 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A block of mass m = 3 kg is pushed up a rough inclined plane of angle 37 by a constant horizontal force F = 60 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is μk = 0.2. What is the absolute magnitude of work done (in Joules) by the force of friction as the block moves a distance of 5 m up the incline? (Take g =10 \(m/s^{2}\) )
questions.solution: Establish a coordinate system with the x-axis parallel to the incline. Resolve the forces perpendicular to the incline to find the normal force N. The component of gravity perpendicular to the incline is mgcos37. The horizontal force F also has a component pressing into the incline: Fsin37. The normal force is N = \(mgcos37 +^{°°}\) Fsin37 = 3(10)(0.8) + 60(0.6) = 24 + 36 = 60 N. The magnitude of the kinetic friction force is fk = μk N = 0.2×60 =12 N. questions.text: Blocks A and B, of masses mA = 3 kg and mB = 2 kg respectively, are placed on a smooth horizontal surface and connected by a light spring. A constant horizontal force F = 20 N is applied to block A, pulling it away from block B. The system starts from rest. At a certain instant, the speed of block A is 4 m/s and the speed of block B is 2 m/s. What is the total work done by ALL forces on the two blocks, during this process, taken together?
questions.solution: According to the Work-Energy Theorem for a system of particles, the total work done by all forces (both external and internal) is exactly equal to the change in the total kinetic energy of the system. The system starts from rest, so the initial kinetic energy is Ki = 0. At the given instant, the final kinetic energy of block A is KA = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(mAvA^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) (3)\((4^{2}\) ) = 24 J. The final kinetic energy of block B is KB = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(mBvB^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) (2)\((2^{2}\) ) = 4 J. The total final kinetic energy of the system is K f = KA + KB = 24 + 4 = 28 J. Therefore, the total work done by all forces is Wtotal = ΔK = 28 J.

questions.text: An electron in a hydrogen-like atom is in a state described by a spatial wavefunction that exhibits exactly 2 angular nodes and 3 radial nodes. What is the principal quantum number n of this state, and what is the total number of degenerate spatial orbitals in the corresponding principal shell?
questions.solution: The number of angular nodes in an atomic orbital corresponds exactly to the azimuthal quantum number l, so l = 2. The number of radial nodes is given by the formula n − l −1. Equating this to 3, we get n − 2 −1 = 3, yielding n = 6. For a hydrogen-like atom (purely Coulombic potential), all subshells within the same principal shell are degenerate. Thus, the total number of degenerate orbitals in the n = 6 shell is \(n^{2}\) = \(6^{2}\) = 36.

questions.text: A sample of hydrogen-like He+ ions is excited to a higher energy state corresponding to the principal quantum number n = 7. If a detector is specifically calibrated to only count the spectral lines that fall exactly within the Paschen series, determine the total number of distinct observable spectral lines registered by this detector.
questions.solution: The Paschen series corresponds to electron transitions terminating at the n = 3 state. For an electron cascading from an initial state of n = 7, the possible downward transitions that terminate exactly at n = 3 are 7 → 3, 6 → 3, 5 → 3, and 4 → 3. questions.text: In a high-precision electron beam lithography system, an electron is accelerated to a nominal velocity of 300m / s. According to the fundamental limits set by Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, what is the theoretical minimum uncertainty in its position, expressed in millimeters (mm)? (Use h = 6.63×\(10^{−34}\) Js, me = 9.1×\(10^{−31}\) kg, π = 3.14 )
questions.solution: From Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, the minimum uncertainty is given by Δx ⋅ mΔv = \(\frac{h}{4π}\). Substituting the given values: Δx = \(\frac{6.63×10^{−34}}{4⋅3.14⋅9.1×10^{−31}⋅0.01}\) Solving this gives Δx ≈ 5.8×\(10^{−3}\) m, which is equal to 5.8mm.

questions.text: A helium-ion ( He+ ) is subjected to intense electromagnetic radiation in a stellar atmosphere, causing its electron to jump from the ground state to the second excited state. questions.solution: KEY The second excited state corresponds to the principal quantum number n = 3. The atomic number for a helium ion is Z = 2. The radius of the n -th orbit for a hydrogen-like species is given by the formula r = a0 \(\frac{n^{2}}{Z}\). Substituting the specific values yields r = a0 \(\frac{3^{2}}{2}\) = 4.5a0.

questions.text: During a crystallographic study of late transition metals, a researcher needs to determine the precise distribution of valence electrons to accurately model the metallic bonding. For an isolated atom of Palladium ( Pd, Atomic Number Z = 46) in its ground state, which of the following accurately represents its outermost electronic configuration?
questions.solution: Palladium ( Pd, Z = 46 ) is a notable exception in the 4d transition metal series. Due to the significant thermodynamic stability gained by having a completely filled d -subshell and the low energy gap between 4d and 5s orbitals, both of the expected 5s electrons are completely transferred to the 4d subshell. Hence, its anomalous ground state configuration is Kr\(4d^{10} 5s^{0}\).

questions.text: An advanced excimer laser apparatus utilized in semiconductor lithography emits a brief, highly focused pulse of ultraviolet radiation with a specific wavelength of 150nm. If internal energy monitors indicate that the entire pulse delivers exactly 5.0×\(10^{10}\) photons to the target surface, calculate the net total energy of this laser pulse in Joules. (Assume Planck's constant h = 6.6×\(10^{−34}\) J ⋅s and the speed of light in vacuum c = 3.0×\(10^{8}\) m / s ).
questions.solution: The energy of a single photon is given by Ephoton = \(\frac{hc}{ℓ}\). Substituting the given values: Ephoton = 6.6×\(\frac{10^{−34}}{150×}\)\(\frac{×3.0}{10^{−9}}\)×\(10^{8}\) = \(\frac{19.8}{150}\)\(\frac{×10^{−26}}{×10^{−9}}\) =1.32×\(10^{−18}\) J. The total energy of the pulse is the energy of one photon multiplied by the total number of photons N: Etotal = N× Ephoton = \((5.0×10^{10}\) )×\((1.32×10^{−18}\) ) = 6.6×\(10^{−8}\) J.

questions.text: According to the postulates of Bohr's semi- classical model for hydrogen-like species, orbiting electrons possess distinct, quantized time periods of revolution. questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: During a seminar on quantum mechanics and the photoelectric effect, a professor lists several propositions regarding the emission of photoelectrons from a metallic cathode under monochromatic illumination. Which of the following statements is fundamentally incorrect?
options: The threshold frequency required to initiate photoelectron emission is an intrinsic characteristic of the metal's work function and is completely independent of the incident light's intensity.

If the frequency of the incident radiation is strictly maintained above the threshold, the magnitude of the saturation photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light.
For a given metallic surface, the slope of the linear plot between the stopping potential and the frequency of incident radiation is a unique characteristic property of that specific metal.

The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectrons depends strictly on the frequency of the incoming electromagnetic wave and the material's work function, regardless of how long the surface is irradiated.
questions.solution: The slope of the graph of stopping potential ( V0 ) versus frequency ( ν ) is obtained from Einstein's photoelectric equation: V0 = \(\frac{h}{e}\) ν − \(\frac{Φ}{e}\). The slope is invariably h, which is a universal constant e (Planck's constant divided by elementary charge). It does not depend on the nature of the specific metal used. The other statements correctly describe the photoelectric effect.

questions.text: The diagram below is a schematic grid representation of a specific continuous block situated within the p -block of the modern long- form periodic table. The atomic number of one central element is explicitly provided as 34 to anchor the grid. Based entirely on the periodic trends and properties of the elements occupying these exact positions, which of the following statements is unequivocally correct?

questions.text: Assume a hypothetical universe where the electron spin quantum number, ms, can take three distinct values ( − \(\frac{1}{2}\),0,+ \(\frac{1}{2}\) ) instead of two. All other quantum mechanical rules, including the allowed values for n, l, and ml, as well as the Aufbau principle and the (n + l) rule, remain identical to those in our universe. Determine the total number of elements that would be present in the \(6^{th}\) period of the modern periodic table in this hypothetical universe.
questions.solution: In the standard universe, the \(6^{th}\) period corresponds to the filling of the 6s,4f,5d, and 6p subshells. The total number of orbitals available in these subshells is 1(for 6s ) +7 (for 4f ) +5 (for 5d ) +3 (for 6p ) = 16 orbitals. If the spin quantum number ms has three permitted values, the modified Pauli exclusion principle dictates that each orbital can accommodate a maximum of 3 electrons. Therefore, the total number of elements in the \(6^{th}\) period would be 16× 3 = 48 elements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Consider the ground state electronic configuration of a Xenon atom ( Z = 54 ). Determine the total number of electrons that simultaneously satisfy the conditions: azimuthal quantum number ℓ ≥1, magnetic quantum number ml = 0, and spin quantum number ms = +1/ 2.
questions.solution: The electronic configuration of Xenon ( Z = 54 ) is \(1s^{2}\)\(2s^{2}\)\(2p^{6}\)\(3s^{2}\)\(3p^{6}\)\(4s^{2}\)\(3d^{10}\)\(4p^{6}\)\(5s^{2}\)\(4d^{10}\)\(5p^{6}\). The condition l ≥1restricts us to the p and d subshells, which are 2p,3p,4p,5p,3d, and 4d. In each of these 6 subshells, there is exactly one orbital corresponding to ml = 0. Since each completely filled orbital holds exactly one electron with ms = +1/ 2, there are exactly 6 such electrons in total.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A sample containing stationary \(Li^{2}\)+ ions in its ground state is irradiated with a beam of monochromatic photons. The ions absorb the photons and are excited to a higher energy level n. During the subsequent de-excitation process to the ground state, the sample emits a total of 10 distinct spectral lines. Let ℓL be the longest wavelength and ℓS be the shortest wavelength among all the spectral lines emitted in this process. Find the value of \(\frac{3ℓL}{ℓS}\).
questions.solution: The number of distinct spectral lines is given by n(n −1) =10, which implies the excited state is 2 n = 5. The energy of a spectral transition is proportional to ( \(\frac{1}{nf^{2}}\) − \(\frac{1}{ni^{2}}\) ). The longest wavelength ℓL corresponds to the minimum energy transition, which is 5 → 4, giving ΔEmin ∝ (\(\frac{1}{16}\) − \(\frac{1}{25}\) ) = \(\frac{9}{400}\). The shortest wavelength ℓS corresponds to the maximum energy transition, which is 5 →1, giving ΔEmax ∝ (1− \(\frac{1}{25}\) ) = \(\frac{24}{25}\). The ratio of the wavelengths is \(\frac{ℓL}{ℓS}\) = \(\frac{ΔEmax}{ΔEmin}\) = \(\frac{24}{9 /}\) \(\frac{/ 25}{400}\) = \(\frac{128}{3}\), therefore \(\frac{3ℓL}{ℓS}\) =128.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The successive ionization energies (in \(eV.atom^{–1}\)) of an element M belonging to the third period are given as: IE1 = 8.1, IE2 =16.3, IE3 = 33.5, IE4 = 45.1, IE5 =166.8, IE6 = 205.2. Let the group number of M in the modern periodic table be G. In the ground state electronic configuration of M, let x be the total number of completely filled p -orbitals and y be the total number of completely filled s -orbitals. Determine the value of G + (x × y).
questions.solution: There is a massive jump between IE4 and IE5, indicating that element M has 4 valence electrons. Since it belongs to the third period, M is Silicon ( Si ), which is placed in Group 14, so G =14. The ground state electronic configuration of Si is \(1s^{2}\)\(2s^{2}\)\(2p^{6}\)\(3s^{2}\)\(3p^{2}\). The 1s, 2s, and 3s orbitals are completely filled, yielding y = 3. Among the p - orbitals, only the three 2p -orbitals are completely filled (the 3p -orbitals have two unpaired electrons due to Hund's rule), giving x = 3. The required value is 14 + (3×3) = 23.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An inorganic chemist is analyzing the standard electron gain enthalpies ( ΔegH1 ) of several representative elements to identify suitable oxidants. Consider the following specific set of isolated neutral atoms in their ground state: N,O,F, Ne,P,S,Cl,Ar,Be,Mg. Determine the exact number of elements from this set that possess a strictly exothermic first electron gain enthalpy (i.e., ΔegH1 0 ).
questions.solution: CHEMISTRY Elements with an exothermic first electron gain enthalpy readily accept an electron to release energy. In the given list, O,F,P,S, and Cl have negative (exothermic) ΔegH1 values. However, Nitrogen ( N ) has a stable half-filled \(2p^{3}\) configuration, making its electron gain slightly endothermic (positive). The noble gases ( Ne,Ar ) have completely filled shells and thus highly positive ΔegH1. The alkaline earth metals ( Be,Mg ) have completely filled s -subshells, also resulting in positive ΔegH1. Therefore, exactly 5 elements have exothermic values.
